content:
Label the coins as follows:
\[
\begin{array}{ccccc}
&&A\\
&B&&C\\
D&&E&&F
\end{array}
\]

### Showing that two moves are enough
Keep coins \(B,C,D,F\) fixed. If \(D\) and \(F\) become the leftmost and rightmost coins of the circle, then \(B\) and \(C\) already occupy the two upper positions of the circle.

Move:
- \(A\) to one of the two lower positions, and
- \(E\) to the other lower position.

Thus all six coins form the required ring, using only two moved coins.

### Showing that one move is impossible
If only one coin were moved, five original coin centers would remain fixed. Removing any one coin from the triangle leaves three coins along at least one side of the large triangle still collinear.

However, the centers of the six coins in the final circle are vertices of a regular hexagon, all lying on one circle. A circle cannot contain three distinct collinear points. Therefore one moved coin cannot suffice.

Hence the smallest possible number is
\[
\boxed{2}
\]
